lead: Landing gear carries the aircraft on the ground, and the brakes stop it. The gear uses an oleo strut: a cylinder of nitrogen gas acts as a spring, and oil forced through a small hole acts as a damper. The brakes turn the aircraft's kinetic energy into heat, so their design is really a heat problem. Every landing and every rejected takeoff depends on the two working together.
prereq: You need the hydraulic supply and actuator ideas from hydraulic systems.

sections.h3: Gear layout and the oleo strut

blocks.text: Landing gear is classified first by whether it moves. Fixed gear stays out, and light aircraft use it because it is simple and light. Retractable gear folds away in flight to cut drag, and it costs actuators, locks and doors. Gear is also classed by layout: nose wheel or tail wheel, and main gear with a single wheel, multiple wheels, or a bogie (a beam carrying two or more wheel pairs). A nose-wheel layout is stable on the ground; a tail-wheel layout is lighter but tends to swing.

Shock absorbers are classed by what stores the landing energy: a rigid gear leaves it to the tyres; light aircraft use a spring-steel leg or rubber bungee cords; almost every larger aircraft uses the oleo-pneumatic strut. The oleo strut does two jobs with one cylinder. Nitrogen above the oil is the spring: it compresses, stores the landing energy, then pushes the aircraft back up. Oil is the damper: as the strut closes, oil is forced through an orifice, often shaped by a metering pin, and the oil turns bounce energy into heat. Gas alone would bounce like a ball; oil alone would not spring back. A static seal joins parts that never move against each other; a dynamic seal rides on the sliding piston and keeps oil in and dirt out.

blocks.where: F is the upward force from the strut in newtons (N), p is the nitrogen pressure in pascals (Pa), and A is the piston area in square metres (m²). A larger piston or higher pressure carries a heavier aircraft.

blocks.text: Tyres are the only contact with the runway. They are tubeless on most aircraft, inflated with nitrogen to reduce fire risk, and checked cold because pressure rises with heat. Each tyre has a rated load, so a bogie spreads the aircraft weight over more tyres and lowers the runway strength needed.

sections.h3: Retraction, locks and the squat switch

blocks.text: A hydraulic actuator pushes the gear down or pulls it up; on some aircraft an electric motor drives the same linkage. Main legs usually swing sideways into the wing root or fuselage, or fore and aft into an engine nacelle; nose legs swing forward or aft. A side brace (drag brace) folds as the leg swings and is held straight by an over-centre lock when the leg is down. An uplock catches the gear in the up position so it cannot fall out, and a downlock holds the brace straight so the leg cannot fold on landing. The downlock matters most at touchdown: a gear that is down but not locked can collapse.

Sequence keeps the aircraft safe. The selector sends a command, the doors open, the gear moves, the doors close, and sensors confirm each position. A squat switch (weight-on-wheels switch) on the gear leg senses that the aircraft is on the ground and blocks retraction. Without it, a pilot could select gear up while parked. The same switch also arms other ground-only logic.

items: Uplock: holds gear up, released before extension.
Downlock: holds gear down, released before retraction.
Squat switch: says the aircraft is on the ground and stops retraction.
Proximity sensor: tells the cockpit the gear is actually locked, not just commanded.

blocks.text: Gear position indication and the logic that sequences gear with flaps are covered in landing gear and flap control. The pressure that drives the actuators comes from the hydraulic system.

A brake is an energy converter. It takes the aircraft's kinetic energy and turns it into heat in the discs. Single-disc brakes suit light aircraft; multi-disc brakes stack several discs to get more friction area in a small wheel. Carbon-carbon discs are used on large aircraft because they are light and survive very high temperatures. Steel discs are cheaper and work well at lower energy.

blocks.where: E is kinetic energy in joules (J), m is aircraft mass in kilograms (kg), and v is landing speed in metres per second (m/s). Because v is squared, a small increase in speed raises brake energy a lot.

blocks.text: On light aircraft each brake pedal works a master cylinder, as in a car. On transports the pedals move a brake metering valve that admits system pressure to the brake pistons; an alternate hydraulic system and an accumulator back it up, and a shuttle valve connects the brake to whichever supply is live. Antiskid works like this: a wheel speed sensor measures each wheel. If a wheel slows too fast, it is about to skid, so the antiskid valve releases pressure for a moment and lets the wheel spin up again. This keeps friction near its best value and protects the tyre. Autobrake holds a selected deceleration after touchdown, and the parking brake holds the aircraft on accumulator pressure when the pumps are off.

Brake temperature is a real limit. Carbon discs can glow after a rejected takeoff, and fusible plugs in the wheel melt to let the tyre deflate before it can burst. Some syllabi list rocket separation mechanisms beside landing gear, because both are mechanisms driven by stored energy. A rocket stage is held by explosive bolts, frangible nuts or a clamp band (a Marman clamp) that a pyrotechnic charge releases; springs, gas pistons or small separation rockets then push the stages apart.

examples.question: A 60 000 kg aircraft touches down at 250 km/h. Its four main-wheel brakes absorb 60 % of the kinetic energy, shared equally. Find the landing speed in m/s, the total kinetic energy, and the energy taken by each main brake.
steps: Brake share: E_brakes = 0.60 × 144.7 = 86.8 MJ. The other 40 % goes to reverse thrust, aerodynamic drag and rolling resistance.
Each of four brakes: E_one = 86.8 / 4 = 21.7 MJ.
examples.answer: The landing speed is 69.4 m/s, the total kinetic energy is 145 MJ, and each main brake absorbs 21.7 MJ.

examples.question: A 60 000 kg aircraft stands with 92 % of its weight on its two main legs. Each main oleo has a gas piston of diameter 0.20 m and a static gas volume of 4.0 L. Find the static gas pressure. At touchdown a strut is compressed until the gas volume is 1.6 L; taking the gas as isothermal for a first estimate, find the new pressure and the strut force.
steps: Load on one main leg: W = 0.46 × 60 000 × 9.81 = 270 756 N.
Static pressure: p = W ÷ A = 270 756 ÷ 0.031 42 = 8.62 × 10⁶ Pa = 86.2 bar.
Strut force: F = p₂ × A = 215.5 × 10⁵ × 0.031 42 = 677 kN, which is 2.5 times the static load.
examples.answer: Static pressure 86.2 bar; at 1.6 L the gas reaches 215.5 bar and the strut pushes with 677 kN. The gas spring stiffens as it closes, and a fast landing stroke is nearer adiabatic, which gives an even higher pressure.

traps: Swapping the oleo roles: nitrogen gas is the spring, oil is the damper, not the other way round.
Forgetting that brake energy rises with the square of speed: a 10 % faster landing gives 1.1² = 1.21, about 21 % more heat.
Confusing uplock with downlock. The downlock holds the gear rigidly in the down position so the leg cannot fold at touchdown.
Thinking antiskid increases braking pressure. It releases pressure to stop a wheel skidding.
Using the tyre or strut gauge pressure as the force. Force is pressure times piston area, F = pA, and the gas pressure rises as the strut closes, so the static value is only the starting point.

quiz.q: In an oleo strut, which part is the spring and which part is the damper?
quiz.a: Nitrogen gas is the spring; oil forced through an orifice is the damper.

quiz.q: Why does an aircraft need both an uplock and a downlock?
quiz.a: The uplock holds the gear safely in the up position so it cannot fall out. The downlock holds the gear rigidly down so it cannot fold at touchdown. Each lock works in one end position only.

quiz.q: A 40 000 kg aircraft lands at 200 km/h. Find its kinetic energy in MJ.
Why is brake energy more critical in a rejected takeoff than in a normal landing?
quiz.a: At takeoff the aircraft is near maximum mass and may be above landing speed, so E = ½mv² is much larger. The brakes must absorb all of it in one stop, with little cooling time, so disc temperature and wear become the limiting design case.

quiz.q: What does the antiskid system do when a wheel slows too fast?
quiz.a: It releases brake pressure at that wheel so the wheel can spin up again, preventing a skid and keeping tyre friction near its best value.

quiz.q: An aircraft has 80 MJ of kinetic energy at touchdown. The four main brakes take 60 % of it equally. Find the energy per brake.
quiz.a: Brake total = 0.60 × 80 = 48 MJ. Per brake = 48 / 4 = 12 MJ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large aircraft are moving from hydraulic brakes to electric brake actuation, where motors press the discs and remove the hydraulic lines from the wheel bay. Carbon brake wear is now monitored by brake temperature and wear sensors rather than fixed schedules. Search for carbon-carbon aircraft brakes, electric braking on the Boeing 787, and brake temperature monitoring if you want to go deeper.
